faqs.q: An opossum is living under my Cape May Court House deck — should I be worried?
faqs.a: Mostly about the mess, not disease: opossums are not on New Jersey's high-risk rabies list, and they are placid, slow animals that would rather play dead than fight. The marsh-edge streets west of the village produce steady opossum calls, usually an animal that has upgraded from nightly visitor to tenant under a low deck. They do shred insulation and vent ducts when they den in a crawlspace, so we take them out, clean up what they left, and screen the deck or crawlspace opening with buried hardware cloth. Check for young in the pouch season before assuming it is a solo tenant.

faqs.q: Do you charge to inspect a Cape May Court House attic?
faqs.a: The inspection is the working visit: roofline, attic, and foundation get checked, entries get photographed, and you receive a written quote for the full job. Middle Township inspections cover the crawlspace as standard, because in this ground the under-house entries outnumber the roof ones. That sequence — inspect first, quote in writing, then remove and seal — is how every job here runs, so there are no surprise line items after the animals are already out.

Cape May Court House.wildlife_intro:
Cape May Court House is the working center of Middle Township: the old village around the courthouse and Route 9, postwar neighborhoods behind it, and marsh and bayshore a short drive in every direction. Unlike the island towns, most houses here are lived in all year, and the housing mixes older farmhouses and capes with newer subdivisions. Raccoons work the chimneys and the crawlspaces near the marsh edge, bats summer in the village attics, opossums and skunks den under decks, and nonvenomous snakes slide out of the wetlands into foundation plantings all summer.

Crawlspaces collect problems quietly. A vent screen rusts through, a pipe penetration was never sealed, and within a season the space underneath the house holds opossums, skunks, or a raccoon latrine — along with the odor that rides the ductwork upstairs. The fix starts with a light and a full circuit underneath: every vent screened in metal, gaps around plumbing and wiring sealed, and any carcass or waste taken out. Where moisture is part of the draw, we say so plainly, because a damp crawlspace keeps attracting animals no matter how well it is screened. Court House crawlspaces sit close to a high water table, so vent screening here is specified for wet conditions and checked for the rot that comes with them.

faqs.q: There is heavy thumping in my Ocean City attic at night — is it a raccoon?
faqs.a: Heavy, deliberate thumping after dark is the classic raccoon signature; squirrels sound lighter and keep daytime hours. On the island the thumping is usually discovered by a cleaning crew or a neighbor, weeks after the raccoon moved in, which is why Ocean City jobs so often include real cleanup rather than a simple removal. We locate the entry — often a pushed-up soffit or a vent the animal has peeled back — check for a litter before anything moves, and get the family out together. Because raccoons sit on New Jersey's rabies-vector list, droppings and latrine areas in the attic get treated as contaminated material, not swept aside.

faqs.q: Birds nest in my Ocean City bathroom vent every spring — what can be done?
faqs.a: Usually European starlings or house sparrows, the two species New Jersey's Game Code lets us deal with directly when they damage property. The nest comes out, the vent gets cleaned of the mites and debris nests carry, and a proper vent cover with a screen behind it ends the annual tenancy. Ocean City's rental stock gives starlings a vent on every duplex, and the spring nesting rush hits houses whose owners will not arrive until June; a screened cover in the fall is the whole answer. Native birds are a different matter — a chimney swift or swallow nest means timing and deterrence work only, and we will tell you honestly which bird you have before anything is touched.

Ocean City.wildlife_intro:
Ocean City is a barrier-island city of raised houses, most of them rentals or second homes that sit empty for long stretches between summer weeks. That vacancy is the wildlife story here. A raccoon that enters a closed house in October may not be discovered until the owners open up in May; bats colonize the quiet roof voids of the older ocean-side homes, and opossums and skunks settle into the shaded, sandy crawl areas beneath houses on pilings from the Gardens to Corson's Inlet. Birds nest in the vents of houses nobody is watching.

Empty houses invite quiet tenants. A home closed for the winter gives raccoons and bats months of undisturbed tenure, and the damage is usually discovered in a single bad hour at spring opening: fouled insulation, stained ceilings, a chimney full of nesting. Pre-closing walk-throughs in the fall — caps checked, vents screened, gaps at the waterline and roofline sealed — cost far less than post-winter remediation. For owners who are away, a neighbor or caretaker holding a key is the next best thing; small leaks and small entries both grow in an empty house. Ocean City's best wildlife work happens in the fall closing walk-through, and the report we leave is written for an owner who may be three states away when they read it.

faqs.q: We keep catching rats around our Wildwood home — why do they come back?
faqs.a: Because the route and the restaurant are still open. Norway rats commute along fence lines, ivy, and utility runs, and they stay where trash, pet food, or a bird feeder feeds them every single night. Behind Wildwood's food blocks the rat pressure is structural, not personal: shared alleys, dumpster rows, and older sewer laterals, so the residential plan starts with the building's own entries and food storage. We map the runs, seal the building entries in metal and mortar — rats gnaw through foam and wood — and go over the sanitation changes that make the property stop paying out. Trapping alone, without those two halves, is a subscription, not a solution.

faqs.q: I found bat droppings in my Wildwood attic — what happens next?
faqs.a: First we confirm the colony's size and find every entry, which is usually a cluster of small gaps at the ridge, a gable vent, or lifted flashing rather than one obvious hole. The older east-side attics are the island's roosts, and droppings found at spring opening usually mean the colony has been in residence, undisturbed, since the house was closed. Exclusion happens inside the NJ Fish & Wildlife guideline windows — April 1 to May 14 or August 1 to October 15 — using one-way exits, and the guano cleanup afterward is handled as a health material, bagged out rather than swept into the air.

Wildwood.wildlife_intro:
Wildwood's year-round neighborhoods hide behind the boardwalk's summer face: older cottages and small Victorians on the east side, postwar homes and motels-turned-residences toward the bay, and a lot of housing that sits closed from Labor Day to Memorial Day. Raccoons are the island's chief tenants, denning in the crawl areas and chimneys of closed houses. Rats work the blocks behind the food businesses, bats take the older attics, and starlings nest in every unguarded vent and sign cabinet along the commercial strips.

Food decides where animals settle. Bird feeders spill seed that feeds rats at night, pet dishes sit out on porches, trash waits in cans a raccoon can open in seconds, and fallen fruit ferments under backyard trees. Removal without changing that menu is a short truce. We go over the property's food map with the homeowner — secured cans, feeders on baffled poles set away from the house, fruit picked up, grills cleaned — because the houses that stay quiet are the ones that stop advertising. The animal work and the housekeeping have to happen together. Wildwood's closing-season inspection is timed for September, when the crowds leave and the raccoons start shopping for winter addresses.

faqs.q: How much should I budget for wildlife work in Cape May?
faqs.a: Budget for three parts rather than one: getting the animals out, closing every entry they used, and cleaning what they left. On a Cape May Victorian the three-part budget has a fourth shadow item, matching historic trim and paint, and the written quote keeps that visible rather than burying it in the sealing line. Skipping the second part is the classic false economy — a cheap removal with open entries is usually a second removal by the next season, and the written quote separates the parts so you can see that plainly.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Cape May chimney?
faqs.a: Yes, and spring families are handled as families. A mother raccoon picks an uncapped flue because it mimics a hollow tree, and pups too young to climb are never sealed in or left behind — we check the flue first, reunite or remove the litter with the mother, and fit a proper cap once the chimney is empty. Decorative Cape May chimneys were built for coal fires, not caps, and their wide flues are exactly what a spring raccoon mother is shopping for; the cap we fit is sized and finished to suit the house. Raccoons are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so the work is done with that caution built in.

Cape May.wildlife_intro:
Cape May's housing is a museum that people live in: several hundred Victorian houses with gingerbread porches, widow's walks, and turreted rooflines, plus the beach cottages of Poverty Beach and the quieter streets of West Cape May's edge. Every ornament is a potential entry. Bats hold long-standing colonies in the big Victorian attics, raccoons den in the decorative chimneys, and starlings work the vents of the Washington Street blocks. The surrounding marsh and the point's famous bird migration keep the whole town in close contact with wildlife.

The attic is where most of the damage hides. Droppings foul insulation until it stops insulating, urine soaks ceiling drywall, and nesting shreds stored boxes and wiring jackets. A proper attic job pairs the removal itself with a cleanup decision — spot-cleaning a light mess, or pulling and replacing badly fouled insulation once the animals are out and the entries are sealed. Bat guano gets handled as a health material, bagged and carried out rather than swept dry. Homeowners see photographs of what we found, so the cleanup scope is a choice, not a surprise. Cape May attic work is planned around the architecture and the colony together; on a listed Victorian, the sealing details are chosen to disappear into the trim.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Villas porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside after dusk and do not block the opening yourself — a skunk sealed in will spray, dig, or die under the porch, and all three are worse than the skunk. Villas porches and steps sit low over sand, and a skunk can excavate a den under a stoop in a single night; by the time the smell announces it, the family may already be moved in. We take skunks out with covered, low-stress handling, then trench and screen the porch perimeter with buried hardware cloth so the next one cannot move in. Skunks are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so distance and calm are the whole technique.

faqs.q: When is wildlife pressure worst in Villas?
faqs.a: Two waves: spring, when raccoon mothers den in chimneys and attics and groundhogs and skunks emerge hungry, and fall, when squirrels and rodents push hard for winter rooms. Summer belongs to bat colonies and mole damage. In Villas the spring wave arrives with the owners: half the early-season calls here are discoveries, animals that took up residence in a quiet house months before anyone came back. The cheapest job is the early one — noise in its first week is usually one animal and one entry; the same job in month three is a family and a cleanup.

Villas.wildlife_intro:
Villas is a bayshore community of small, plain houses: 1950s cottages and ranches on sandy lots a few streets back from Delaware Bay, in Lower Township. Nothing here is fancy, and the wildlife is correspondingly direct. Raccoons den in the crawlspaces and chimneys of houses that sit closed between owners, opossums and skunks live under the sheds and low decks on nearly every street, and bats work the simple gable attics. The nearby Fishing Creek marsh and the bayshore woods keep a constant supply of animals moving through the yards.

Decks and porches fail at ground level. The gap beneath a low deck is dark, dry, and sheltered enough for skunks, opossums, and groundhogs to den in, and lattice alone stops none of them. Lasting work means trenching around the structure and burying galvanized hardware cloth in an L-shape, so an animal digging at the edge meets mesh angled outward underground. Lattice or skirting goes back over the top for looks. It is unglamorous digging, and it is the difference between a den that stays empty and one that fills again every spring. Villas decks and shed floors sit close to sandy ground that digs easily, so screening here is buried deeper than inland standard, and the trench is part of the quote.

faqs.q: A bat got into my living room in North Wildwood — what should I do?
faqs.a: Close the bat in one room, open a window or exterior door in that room, turn off the lights, and let it leave on its own at dusk; never handle it bare-handed. In a closed-for-winter North Wildwood house a bat in the living room in March usually overwintered in the building, and the visit turns into a check of the whole roof void, not just the room. If anyone slept in the room or a pet made contact, call your local health department — they decide whether the bat should be tested. A single bat usually means a gap worth finding, and we can check the rooflines and vents that let it in.

faqs.q: Once the animals are out of my North Wildwood home, how do I keep them out?
faqs.a: Walk the house the way an animal does: roofline first, then vents, then ground level. Chimney cap, metal-backed vent covers, limbs cut back off the roof, trash in lidded cans, and no pet food or open seed stored in the garage. For island homes the fall list is short and specific: cap, vents, the gap where the deck meets the house, and the crawl opening under the raised floor, because those four account for nearly every winter tenancy here. We leave you the entry map from your own job — which gaps were sealed and which aging spots to watch — because the houses that stay quiet are checked each fall, not just fixed once.

North Wildwood.wildlife_intro:
North Wildwood occupies the inlet end of Five Mile Beach: the old Anglesea fishing village streets, blocks of cottages and duplexes, and newer condos looking over Hereford Inlet. Like the rest of the island it empties out in winter, and the animals move in behind the departing owners. Raccoons den under raised houses and in their chimneys, bats take the older Anglesea attics, and starlings and sparrows nest in the vents of closed duplexes. The inlet marsh at the island's tip keeps opossums and skunks circulating through the bay side streets.

Waterfront houses fight moisture on every front. Crawlspaces on pilings, bulkhead walls, and dock structures give raccoons and opossums dry travel lanes straight to the floor system, and salt air eats vent screens and fasteners years faster than it does inland. Materials matter here: stainless and heavy-gauge mesh, sealed penetrations where pipes pass through the foundation, and caps that survive storm wind. Bats favor the warm, still air under raised houses and inside their roof voids. A shore house proofed with inland materials is a shore house scheduled for a second visit. North Wildwood's inlet air corrodes screens and caps fast, so the materials specified here are marine-grade, and the fall check includes fasteners, not just mesh.
